Large-scale nuclear structure calculations for spin-dependent WIMP scattering
with chiral effective field theory currents

Abstract

We perform state-of-the-art large-scale shell-model calculations of the structure factors for elastic spin-dependent WIMP scattering off 129,131Xe, 127I, 73Ge, 19F, 23Na ,27Al, and 29Si. This comprehensive survey covers the nonzero-spin nuclei relevant to direct dark matter detection. We include a pedagogical presentation of the formalism necessary to describe elastic and inelastic WIMP-nucleus scattering. The valence spaces and nuclear interactions employed have been previously used in nuclear structure calculations for these mass regions and yield a good spectroscopic description of these isotopes. We use spin-dependent WIMP-nucleus currents based on chiral effective field theory (EFT) at the one-body level and including the leading long-range two-body currents due to pion exchange, which are predicted in chiral EFT. Results for all structure factors are provided with theoretical error bands due to the nuclear uncertainties of WIMP currents in nuclei.

I Introduction

About 25%25\% of the energy density of our Universe consists of dark matter, a form of matter that rarely interacts with baryons and has eluded direct observation so far [1, 2]. This large-scale problem is closely connected to new physics at the smallest scales, because dark matter candidates arise naturally in extensions of the Standard Model of particle physics [3]. Prominent dark matter candidates are weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs). They are predicted in supersymmetric models, as the lightest supersymmetric particles (typically neutralinos) and also in other Standard Model extensions like models with extra dimensions. WIMPs are especially promising candidates, because they account naturally for the dark matter energy density established by observations [2]. Moreover, WIMPs interact with quarks, and thus with baryonic matter, opening the door to direct dark matter detection via elastic scattering off nuclei [4]. Inferring properties of dark matter from direct detection therefore requires detailed knowledge of the structure factors for WIMP scattering off strongly interacting nuclei.

In this work, we focus on spin-dependent (SD) WIMP scattering [5], which is relevant because WIMPs can carry spin. In particular we assume spin 1/21/2 WIMPs, such as neutralinos or other Majorana fermions. The detection of elastic SD WIMP scattering has been the goal of several past and ongoing experiments [10, 9, 6, 8, 11, 7, 12], using different nonzero-spin nuclei as target, but so far without evidence. Evaluating the response of nuclei to WIMPs is challenging. First, it requires matching the WIMP-quark couplings in a particular supersymmetric model to WIMP-nucleon currents. Because quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is nonperturbative at low energies, this is best achieved using effective theories [13, 14, 15, 16], in which spin-independent and SD interactions generally enter in leading order. Second, the WIMP-nucleus response requires reliable nuclear-structure calculations. This is especially important for SD interactions, because the response depends on how the spin of the nucleus is distributed among nucleons (due to attractive interactions most of the nucleons pair to spin zero). For the isotopes of interest [10, 9, 6, 8, 11, 7, 12], this involves medium-mass to heavier nuclei and is a challenging many-body problem. Previous calculations of SD WIMP scattering off nuclei [5, 19, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23] have relied on phenomenological WIMP-nucleon currents, and are based on nuclear-structure calculations that can be improved with recent advances in nuclear interactions and computing capabilities. This work presents progress on these fronts.

The typical momentum transfers involved in WIMP scattering off nuclei are low and of order of the pion mass. In addition, the typical momenta involved in low-energy nuclear structure are similar. At these momentum scales, chiral EFT provides a systematic expansion in powers of momenta QQ for nuclear forces and for the coupling to external probes, based on the symmetries of QCD [24, 25]. In addition to the coupling through one-body (1b) currents, generally at leading order, two-body (2b) currents enter at higher order and are quantitatively important.

In previous work [15] we have derived the currents for SD WIMP scattering off nuclei based on chiral EFT, including 1b currents and the leading long-range 2b currents due to pion exchange, which are predicted in chiral EFT. As an application, we focused on the scattering off 129,131Xe, as they provide the most stringent limits for WIMP coupling to neutrons [26]. Our results have recently been adopted as benchmark for the XENON100 SD WIMP-nucleon cross-section limits [12], and have also been used in Ref. [27].

More generally, two-body contributions to weak neutral currents have been shown to be key for providing accurate predictions of neutrino-deuteron scattering at solar neutrino energies for SNO [28, 29]. Weak neutral currents based on chiral EFT have been explored for light nuclei and neutrino breakup in core-collapse supernovae [30, 31, 32, 33], and 2b weak charged currents have been shown to provide important contributions to Gamow-Teller transitions and double-beta decays of medium-mass nuclei [34]. Following our previous work [15], Refs. [35, 36] have reported simple prescriptions to approximately include the effects of chiral 2b currents in previous calculations of SD WIMP-nucleus scattering.

This work expands Ref. [15] by presenting state-of-the-art large-scale shell-model calculations that describe the nonzero-spin states of all isotopes that are experimentally relevant for SD WIMP direct detection: 129,131Xe, 127I, 73Ge, 19F, 23Na, 27Al, and 29Si. The nuclear-structure calculations are performed with interactions and valence spaces that have been tested in these mass regions. Based on the calculated ground states, we predict the structure factors for elastic SD WIMP scattering, including chiral 1b and 2b currents with an improved treatment of the momentum-transfer dependence for higher momentum transfers. We provide theoretical error bands due to the uncertainties of WIMP currents in nuclei.

The outline of this article is as follows. In Sec. II, we derive the WIMP currents in nuclei based on chiral EFT. All microscopic inputs needed to compute the structure factors of SD WIMP-nucleus scattering are discussed in Sec. III. Combined with detailed Appendixes, this includes a pedagogical presentation of the formalism necessary to describe elastic and inelastic WIMP-nucleus scattering. In Sec. IV, we present large-scale nuclear-structure calculations that describe the nuclei relevant for SD WIMP direct detection, and compare our results to experiment. We then calculate the structure factors for elastic SD WIMP scattering for all cases using chiral EFT currents. We discuss in detail the role of 2b currents and their uncertainties; the contributions of different multipole operators to the total response; and the issue of proton/neutron versus isoscalar/isovector decompositions of the structure factors. Finally, we summarize in Sec. V and give an outlook for future improvements of the nuclear physics of dark matter detection.

II WIMP-nucleus interactions

II.1 Chiral EFT and WIMP currents

At the WIMP-quark level, the low-momentum-transfer Lagrangian density ℒ{\mathcal{L}} for SD interactions is taken to be an axial-vector–axial-vector coupling [5, 37]:

ℒχSD\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}^{\rm SD}_{\chi} =GF2​∫d3​𝐫​jμ​(𝐫)​JμA​(𝐫)\displaystyle=\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\int d^{3}{\bf r}\,{j}^{\mu}({\bf r}){J}^{A}_{\mu}({\bf r})
=−GF2∫d3𝐫χ¯𝜸γ5χ⋅∑qAqψ¯q𝜸γ5ψq,\displaystyle=-\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\int d^{3}{\bf r}\,\overline{\chi}{\bm{\gamma}}\gamma_{5}\chi\cdot\sum_{q}A_{q}\overline{\psi}_{q}{\bm{\gamma}}\gamma_{5}\psi_{q}\,, (1)

where GFG_{F} is the Fermi coupling constant, and JμA​(𝐫){J}^{A}_{\mu}({\bf r}) and jμ​(𝐫){j}^{\mu}({\bf r}) denote the hadronic current and the leptonic current of the WIMP, respectively. χ\chi is the neutralino field, ψq\psi_{q} are the fields of q=u,d,sq=u,d,s quarks, and AqA_{q} the neutralino-quark coupling constants. The temporal components can be neglected, because the velocities of WIMPs are expected to be nonrelativistic with v/c∼10−3v/c\sim 10^{-3}. We also neglect contributions to the Lagrangian density other than axial-vector currents, such as polar-vector currents, which are suppressed by the momentum transfer over the nucleon mass p/mp/m [5]. This approximation will be studied in a future paper.

For the WIMP-nucleus response, the SD WIMP interaction couples dominantly to a single nucleon, but also to pairs of nucleons. At the one-nucleon level, the quark currents are replaced by their expectation value in the nucleon, leading to 1b axial-vector currents 𝐉i,1​b{\bf J}_{i,{\rm 1b}}. In the nucleus, the currents are summed over all AA nucleons:

∑qAq​ψ¯q​𝜸​γ5​ψq⟶∑i=1A𝐉i,1​b=∑i=1A(𝐉i,1​b0+𝐉i,1​b3),\sum_{q}A_{q}\overline{\psi}_{q}{\bm{\gamma}}\gamma_{5}\psi_{q}\longrightarrow\sum_{i=1}^{A}{\bf J}_{i,{\rm 1b}}=\sum_{i=1}^{A}({\bf J}^{0}_{i,{\rm 1b}}+{\bf J}^{3}_{i,{\rm 1b}})\,, (2)

with the isoscalar 𝐉i,1​b0{\bf J}^{0}_{i,{\rm 1b}} and isovector 𝐉i,1​b3{\bf J}^{3}_{i,{\rm 1b}} parts.

The coupling of the isoscalar part is given by [5]

a0=(Au+Ad)​(Δ​u+Δ​d)+2​As​Δ​s,a_{0}=(A_{u}+A_{d})(\Delta u+\Delta d)+2A_{s}\Delta s\,, (3)

where Δ​u,Δ​d,Δ​s\Delta u,\Delta d,\Delta s are defined as ψ¯q​𝜸​γ5​ψq=Δ​q​𝝈/2\overline{\psi}_{q}{\bm{\gamma}}\gamma_{5}\psi_{q}=\Delta q\,{\bm{\sigma}}/2, with the nucleon spin 𝝈/2{\bm{\sigma}}/2. Therefore, 𝐉i,1​b0=a0​𝝈/2{\bf J}^{0}_{i,{\rm 1b}}=a_{0}\,{\bm{\sigma}}/2, and a0a_{0} receives contributions from the isoscalar combination of the uu and dd quarks to the spin of the nucleon, as well as from the ss quark. Analogously, the isovector coupling can be written as

a1=(Au−Ad)​(Δ​u−Δ​d)=(Au−Ad)​gA,a_{1}=(A_{u}-A_{d})(\Delta u-\Delta d)=(A_{u}-A_{d})g_{A}\,, (4)

where gAg_{A} is the axial coupling constant. This shows that the isovector part 𝐉i,1​b3{\bf J}^{3}_{i,{\rm 1b}} of the axial-vector WIMP-nucleon coupling is identical, up to replacing a1a_{1} by gAg_{A}, to the axial-vector part of the weak neutral current.

II.2 Coupling to one nucleon

The weak neutral current was derived within chiral EFT for calculations of low-energy electroweak reactions. At lowest orders Q0Q^{0} and Q2Q^{2}, there are only 1b currents. For the isovector part of the axial-vector WIMP-nucleon current, this leads to [15]

𝐉i,1​b3=12a1τi3(gA​(p2)gA𝝈i−gP​(p2)2​m​gA(𝐩⋅𝝈i)𝐩),{\bf J}^{3}_{i,{\rm 1b}}=\frac{1}{2}\,a_{1}\tau_{i}^{3}\biggl(\frac{g_{A}(p^{2})}{g_{A}}\,{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}-\frac{g_{P}(p^{2})}{2mg_{A}}\,({\bf p}\cdot{\bm{\sigma}}_{i})\,{\bf p}\biggl)\,, (5)

where τi3\tau_{i}^{3} denotes the isospin, 𝐩=𝐩i−𝐩i′{\bf p}={\bf p}_{i}-{\bf p}_{i}^{\prime} the momentum transfer from nucleons to neutralinos, and gA​(p2)g_{A}(p^{2}) and gP​(p2)g_{P}(p^{2}) the axial and pseudo-scalar couplings. The momentum transfer dependence of gA​(p2)g_{A}(p^{2}) and gP​(p2)g_{P}(p^{2}) is due to loop corrections and pion propagators. To order Q2Q^{2}, one has [38]

gA​(p2)gA\displaystyle\frac{g_{A}(p^{2})}{g_{A}} =1−2​p2ΛA2,\displaystyle=1-2\,\frac{p^{2}}{\Lambda_{A}^{2}}\,, (6)
gP​(p2)\displaystyle g_{P}(p^{2}) =2​gπ​p​n​Fπmπ2+p2−4​m​gAΛA2,\displaystyle=\frac{2g_{\pi pn}F_{\pi}}{m_{\pi}^{2}+p^{2}}-4\,\frac{mg_{A}}{\Lambda_{A}^{2}}\,, (7)

with ΛA=1040​MeV\Lambda_{A}=1040\,\text{MeV}, pion mass mπ=138.04​MeVm_{\pi}=138.04\,\text{MeV}, pion decay constant Fπ=92.4​MeVF_{\pi}=92.4\,\text{MeV}, and gπ​p​n=13.05g_{\pi pn}=13.05. Chiral 1b currents are similar to the currents used in previous calculations of WIMP scattering off nuclei [5]. The differences are that the 1/ΛA21/\Lambda_{A}^{2} terms were neglected and the Goldberger-Treiman relation was implicitly used to write gP​(p2)2​m​gA≈1mπ2+p2\frac{g_{P}(p^{2})}{2mg_{A}}\approx\frac{1}{m_{\pi}^{2}+p^{2}}. Both present few percent corrections, but the former increases with momentum transfer.

The axial-vector part of the weak neutral currents is isovector in the Standard Model, neglecting the strange quark contribution to a0a_{0} in Eq. (3). Therefore, higher-order Q2Q^{2} contributions to the isoscalar WIMP-nucleon current 𝐉i,1​b0=a0​𝝈/2{\bf J}^{0}_{i,{\rm 1b}}=a_{0}\,{\bm{\sigma}}/2 depend on models of currents in the nucleon. To order Q2Q^{2}, these lead to 1b currents with a form-factor mass-scale ∼ΛA\sim\Lambda_{A} [39] and without pion propagator contributions. Because the isovector 1/ΛA21/\Lambda_{A}^{2} terms contribute at the few percent level for the typical momentum transfers in WIMP scattering, we chose to neglect higher-order isoscalar current contributions, as opposed to introducing a model dependence at this level.

II.3 Coupling to two nucleons

At order Q3Q^{3}, 2b currents enter in chiral EFT [40]. We consider their long-range parts due to pion exchange, which are predicted in chiral EFT, and for medium-mass nuclei were found to dominate over the short-range parts [15]. Because of their pion-exchange nature, the axial-vector part of the weak neutral 2b current is isovector, 𝐉2​b=∑i<jA𝐉i​j3{\bf J}_{\rm 2b}=\sum^{A}_{i<j}{\bf J}^{3}_{ij}, with

+i𝐩1+𝐩1′4​m+(1+c^64​m)(𝝈1×𝐪)]−(1↔2))\displaystyle\quad+i\,\frac{{{\bf p}_{1}+\bf p}^{\prime}_{1}}{4m}+\Bigl(\frac{1+\hat{c}_{6}}{4m}\Bigr)({\bm{\sigma}}_{1}\times{\bf q})\biggr]-(1\leftrightarrow 2)\Biggr)

where 𝐤i=𝐩i′−𝐩i{\bf k}_{i}={\bf p}^{\prime}_{i}-{\bf p}_{i} and 𝐪=−𝐤1−𝐤2{\bf q}=-{\bf k}_{1}-{\bf k}_{2}. This improves the treatment of the momentum-transfer dependence compared to our previous work [15], as it does not make the approximation of low-momentum transfers in the currents [40]. As a result, two momentum transfers appear, 𝐤1{\bf k}_{1} and 𝐤2{\bf k}_{2}, and also a new term proportional to 1+c^61+\hat{c}_{6}, which vanishes in the limit of zero momentum transfer.

As in Ref. [15], we take into account the normal-ordered one-body part of chiral 2b currents. This is obtained by summing the second nucleon jj over occupied states in a spin and isospin symmetric reference state or core, which we take as a Fermi gas: 𝐉i,2​beff=∑j(1−Pi​j)​𝐉i​j3{\bf J}^{\rm eff}_{i,{\rm 2b}}=\sum_{j}(1-P_{ij}){\bf J}^{3}_{ij}. The exchange operator Pi​jP_{ij} includes all two-body exchange contributions. Normal ordering is expected to be a very good approximation for medium-mass and heavy nuclei, because of phase-space restrictions of normal Fermi systems at low energies [41].

The contributions from 2b currents in Eqs. (9)–(13) depend on the density of the reference state ρ=2​kF3/(3​π2)\rho=2k_{\rm F}^{3}/(3\pi^{2}) (kFk_{\rm F} is the Fermi momentum) and on the low-energy couplings c3c_{3}, c4c_{4}, and c^6\hat{c}_{6}. To be conservative, we also consider the estimated uncertainty in these values expected from higher-order order contributions, δ​c3=−δ​c4≈1​GeV−1\delta c_{3}=-\delta c_{4}\approx 1\,\text{GeV}^{-1} [24]. The resulting c3c_{3} and c4c_{4} values are given in Tables 1 and 2. We take c^6=5.83\hat{c}_{6}=5.83 from Ref. [46].

In Table 1, we study the PP dependence of the 2b current contribution to the axial coupling, which we write as 𝐉i,2beff,σ​(ρ,P)=−gA​𝝈i​τi32​ρFπ2​Jσ​(ρ,P){\bf J}^{\text{eff},\sigma}_{i,\text{2b}}(\rho,P)=-g_{A}{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}\frac{\tau^{3}_{i}}{2}\frac{\rho}{F^{2}_{\pi}}J^{\sigma}(\rho,P), at p=0p=0. Table 1 shows that the PP dependence is very weak: Jσ​(ρ,0)J^{\sigma}(\rho,0) varies by less than 12% over the relevant PP range. For other densities in the range ρ=0.10​…​0.12​fm−3\rho=0.10...0.12\,{\rm fm}^{-3} this variation is even smaller. Because 2b currents are a correction to the leading 1b currents, we therefore set P=0P=0 in the axial 2b current contribution, Eq. (9). As the contributions from Eqs. (11)–(13) are expected to be weaker, we therefore consistently set P=0P=0, so that only the standard pseudo-scalar part, Eq. (10), contributes. Finally to connect to our previous work, for p=P=0p=P=0, both I1σI^{\sigma}_{1} and I2σI^{\sigma}_{2} lead to [15]

Iσ(ρ,p=P=0)\displaystyle I^{\sigma}(\rho,p=P=0) ≡I1σ(ρ,p=P=0)=I2σ(ρ,p=P=0)\displaystyle\equiv I^{\sigma}_{1}(\rho,p=P=0)=I^{\sigma}_{2}(\rho,p=P=0)
=1−3​mπ2kF2+3​mπ3kF3​arctan⁡(kFmπ),\displaystyle=1-\frac{3m_{\pi}^{2}}{k_{\text{F}}^{2}}+\frac{3m_{\pi}^{3}}{k_{\text{F}}^{3}}\arctan\biggl(\frac{k_{\text{F}}}{m_{\pi}}\biggr), (14)

where Iσ(ρ,p=P=0)=0.58…0.60I^{\sigma}(\rho,p=P=0)=0.58...0.60 depends only weakly on the density in the range ρ=0.10​…​0.12​fm−3\rho=0.10...0.12\,{\rm fm}^{-3}.

For P=0P=0, the 2b current contribution to the axial part, Eq. (9), can be written as a momentum- and density-dependent renormalization δ​a1​(p)\delta a_{1}(p),

𝐉i,2beff,σ=gA​𝝈i​τi32​δ​a1​(p),{\bf J}^{\text{eff},\sigma}_{i,\text{2b}}=g_{A}{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}\frac{\tau^{3}_{i}}{2}\,\delta a_{1}(p)\,,\\ (15)

with

δ​a1​(p)=\displaystyle\delta a_{1}(p)= −ρFπ2[13(c4+14​m)[3I2σ(ρ,p)−I1σ(ρ,p)]\displaystyle-\frac{\rho}{F^{2}_{\pi}}\,\biggl[\frac{1}{3}\Bigl(c_{4}+\frac{1}{4m}\Bigr)\Bigl[3I_{2}^{\sigma}(\rho,p)-I_{1}^{\sigma}(\rho,p)\Bigr]
+13(−c3+14​m)I1σ(ρ,p)−(1+c^612​m)Ic6(ρ,p)].\displaystyle+\frac{1}{3}\Bigl(-c_{3}+\frac{1}{4m}\Bigr)I_{1}^{\sigma}(\rho,p)-\Bigl(\frac{1+\hat{c}_{6}}{12m}\Bigr)I_{c_{6}}(\rho,p)\biggl]\,. (16)

Similarly, we write the 2b-current contribution to the pseudo-scalar coupling, Eq. (10), as a momentum- and density-dependent renormalization δ​a1P​(p)\delta a_{1}^{P}(p),

𝐉i,2beff,P=gA​τi32​(𝐩⋅𝝈i)​𝐩​δ​a1P​(p)p2,{\bf J}^{\text{eff},P}_{i,\text{2b}}=g_{A}\,\frac{\tau^{3}_{i}}{2}\,({\bf p}\cdot{\bm{\sigma}}_{i})\,{\bf p}\,\frac{\delta a_{1}^{P}(p)}{p^{2}}\,, (17)

with

δ​a1P​(p)\displaystyle\delta a_{1}^{P}(p) =ρFπ2[−2​c3​p2mπ2+p2+c3+c43IP(ρ,p)\displaystyle=\frac{\rho}{F^{2}_{\pi}}\biggl[\frac{-2c_{3}p^{2}}{m^{2}_{\pi}+p^{2}}+\frac{c_{3}+c_{4}}{3}\,I^{P}(\rho,p)
−1+c^612​mIc6(ρ,p)].\displaystyle\quad-\frac{1+\hat{c}_{6}}{12m}\,I_{c_{6}}(\rho,p)\biggr]\,. (18)

The ranges of δ​a1​(p)\delta a_{1}(p) and δ​a1P​(p)\delta a_{1}^{P}(p) are given in Table 2 for the c3,c4c_{3},c_{4} values and the density range considered. We find that δ​a1​(p)\delta a_{1}(p) reduces the axial part of the current by 14%​…​32%14\%...32\% at p=0p=0. The momentum transfer dependence is mild, as the reduction is 16%​…​36%16\%...36\% at p=mπp=m_{\pi}. Moreover, δ​a1P​(p)\delta a_{1}^{P}(p) increases the pseudo-scalar part of the current by 23%​…​54%23\%...54\% at p=mπp=m_{\pi}. At lower momentum transfers this enhancement is weaker, while it is more significant for higher pp. These results are consistent with studies of Gamow-Teller transitions and double-beta decays [34]. As discussed in Ref. [15], in addition to the long-range 2b pion-exchange currents, there are short-range 2b currents for the isoscalar and isovector parts, which are included as contact terms in chiral EFT. The isovector short-range 2b parts only lead to small contributions [34]. Therefore, we neglect short-range 2b currents at this level, which is also consistent with neglecting higher-order (short-range) 1b isoscalar currents, see Sec. II.2.

II.4 Combined response

Combining the 1b and the long-range 2b currents to order Q3Q^{3} in chiral EFT (replacing gAg_{A} by a1a_{1} for the latter), the isovector part of the axial-vector WIMP current at the normal-ordered one-body level is given by [15]

𝐉i,1​b+2​b3\displaystyle{\bf J}^{3}_{i,{\rm 1b+2b}} =12a1τi3[(gA​(p2)gA+δa1(p))𝝈i\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\,a_{1}\tau_{i}^{3}\Biggl[\biggl(\frac{g_{A}(p^{2})}{g_{A}}+\delta a_{1}(p)\biggr)\,{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}
+(−gP​(p2)2​m​gA+δ​a1P​(p)p2)(𝐩⋅𝝈i)𝐩].\displaystyle\quad+\biggl(-\frac{g_{P}(p^{2})}{2mg_{A}}+\frac{\delta a_{1}^{P}(p)}{p^{2}}\biggr)\,({\bf p}\cdot{\bm{\sigma}}_{i})\,{\bf p}\,\Biggr]\,. (19)

III WIMP-nucleus scattering and structure factors

III.1 WIMP-nucleus scattering

The differential cross section for SD WIMP elastic scattering off a nucleus in the initial state |i⟩\ket{i} to the final state |f⟩\ket{f} can be obtained from the low-momentum-transfer Lagrangian density of Eq. (1). A detailed derivation is performed in Appendix B. The final result is [5]

d​σd​p2\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma}{dp^{2}} =2(2​Ji+1)​π​v2​∑sf,si∑Mf,Mi|⟨f|​ℒχSD​|i⟩|2\displaystyle=\frac{2}{(2J_{i}+1)\pi v^{2}}\sum_{s_{f},s_{i}}\sum_{M_{f},M_{i}}\bigl|\bra{f}{\mathcal{L}}^{\rm SD}_{\chi}\ket{i}\bigr|^{2}
=8​GF2(2​Ji+1)​v2​SA​(p),\displaystyle=\frac{8G^{2}_{F}}{(2J_{i}+1)v^{2}}\,S_{A}(p)\,, (20)

where the sum sf,si=±1/2s_{f},s_{i}=\pm 1/2 is over neutralino spin projections, and the sum Mf,MiM_{f},M_{i} is over the projections of the total angular momentum of the final and initial states Jf,JiJ_{f},J_{i}, respectively; vv is the WIMP velocity, and SA​(p)S_{A}(p) the axial-vector structure factor. The structure factor can be decomposed as a sum over multipoles LL with reduced matrix elements of the longitudinal ℒL5{\mathcal{L}}^{5}_{L}, transverse electric 𝒯Lel5{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{el}5}_{L}, and transverse magnetic 𝒯Lmag5{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{mag}5}_{L} projections of the axial-vector currents:

SA​(p)=\displaystyle S_{A}(p)= ∑L⩾0|⟨Jf||​ℒL5​||Ji⟩|2+∑L⩾1(|⟨Jf||​𝒯Lel5​||Ji⟩|2CLOSE\displaystyle\sum_{L\geqslant 0}\bigl|\bra{J_{f}}\!|{\mathcal{L}}_{L}^{5}|\!\ket{J_{i}}\bigr|^{2}+\sum_{L\geqslant 1}\Bigl(\bigl|\bra{J_{f}}\!|{\mathcal{T}}_{L}^{\mathrm{el}5}|\!\ket{J_{i}}\bigr|^{2}
OPEN+|⟨Jf||​𝒯Lmag5​||Ji⟩|2).\displaystyle+\bigl|\bra{J_{f}}\!|{\mathcal{T}}_{L}^{\mathrm{mag}5}|\!\ket{J_{i}}\bigr|^{2}\Bigr)\,. (21)

The multipole contributions are obtained from the WIMP-nucleus currents 𝐉A​(𝐫){\bf J}^{A}({\bf r}). At the effective one-body level, chiral 1b and 2b currents lead to (see Appendix B for the definition of the multipole operators and details of the derivation)

ℒL5​(p)=\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{L}^{5}(p)= i2​L+1∑i=1A12[a0+a1τi3(1+δa1(p)\displaystyle\frac{i}{\sqrt{2L+1}}\sum^{A}_{i=1}\frac{1}{2}\biggl[a_{0}+a_{1}\tau^{3}_{i}\Bigl(1+\delta a_{1}(p)
−2​gπ​p​n​Fπ​p22​m​gA​(p2+mπ2)+δa1P(p))]\displaystyle-\frac{2g_{\pi pn}F_{\pi}p^{2}}{2mg_{A}(p^{2}+m^{2}_{\pi})}+\delta a_{1}^{P}(p)\Bigr)\biggr]
×[L+1​ML,L+1​(p​𝐫i)+L​ML,L−1​(p​𝐫i)],\displaystyle\times\!\Bigl[\sqrt{L+1}M_{L,L+1}(p{\bf r}_{i})+\sqrt{L}M_{L,L-1}(p{\bf r}_{i})\Bigr], (22)
𝒯Lel5​(p)=\displaystyle{\mathcal{T}}_{L}^{\mathrm{el}5}(p)= i2​L+1\displaystyle\frac{i}{\sqrt{2L+1}}
×∑i=1A12​[a0+a1​τi3​(1−2​p2ΛA2+δ​a1​(p))]\displaystyle\times\sum^{A}_{i=1}\frac{1}{2}\biggl[a_{0}+a_{1}\tau^{3}_{i}\Bigl(1-2\frac{p^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}_{A}}+\delta a_{1}(p)\Bigr)\biggr]
×[−L​ML,L+1​(p​𝐫i)+L+1​ML,L−1​(p​𝐫i)],\displaystyle\times\Bigl[-\sqrt{L}M_{L,L+1}(p{\bf r}_{i})+\sqrt{L+1}M_{L,L-1}(p{\bf r}_{i})\Bigr], (23)

×ML,L​(p​𝐫i).\displaystyle\times M_{L,L}(p{\bf r}_{i})\,. (24)

The matrix elements of the operator ML,L′​(p​𝐫i)=jL′​(p​ri)​[YL′​(𝐫^i)​𝝈i]LM_{L,L^{\prime}}(p{\bf r}_{i})=j_{L^{\prime}}(pr_{i})[Y_{L^{\prime}}(\hat{\bf r}_{i})\,{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}]^{L} (with L′L^{\prime} and 𝝈{\bm{\sigma}} coupled to LL) are given in Appendix C.

III.2 Parity constraints

The different multipoles in Eqs. (22)–(24) have well-defined parity Π\Pi, which can be deduced from the definitions given in Appendix B, Eqs. (55)–(57), and the transformations under parity of

Π⁡(∇)=−1,\displaystyle\Pi({\bm{\nabla}})=-1\,, Π⁡(YL​M)=(−1)L,\displaystyle\Pi(Y_{LM})=(-1)^{L}\,, Π⁡(𝐘L​L​1M)=(−1)L,\displaystyle\Pi({\bf Y}^{M}_{LL1})=(-1)^{L}\,,

and the parity of axial-vector one-body currents Π⁡(𝐉A)=+1\Pi({\bf J}^{A})=+1. For elastic scattering, where the initial and final states of the nucleus are identical (J=Ji=JfJ=J_{i}=J_{f}), only the multipoles with positive parity (Π=+1\Pi=+1) contribute to the structure factor, so that we have

Π⁡(ℒL5)=(−1)L+1\displaystyle\Pi({\mathcal{L}}_{L}^{5})=(-1)^{L+1} ⇒L​ odd,\displaystyle\Rightarrow\quad L\text{ odd}\,,
Π⁡(𝒯Lel5)=(−1)L+1\displaystyle\Pi({\mathcal{T}}_{L}^{\mathrm{el}5})=(-1)^{L+1} ⇒L​ odd,\displaystyle\Rightarrow\quad L\text{ odd}\,,
Π⁡(𝒯Lmag5)=(−1)L\displaystyle\Pi({\mathcal{T}}_{L}^{\mathrm{mag}5})=(-1)^{L} ⇒L​ even.\displaystyle\Rightarrow\quad L\text{ even}\,.

Hence, for elastic scattering only the odd-LL multipoles of the longitudinal and transverse electric operators and only the even-LL multipoles of the transverse magnetic operator contribute. This is also the case for inelastic scattering between initial and final states of the same parity. For inelastic scattering involving different parity states, the above constraints get reversed.

III.3 Time-reversal constraints

For elastic scattering, time-reversal invariance also constrains the multipoles that contribute to the structure factor. We can write the reduced matrix elements of the sum over one-body operators OL​(i)O_{L}(i) as [13]

⟨J⁡∥∑i=1AOL​(i)∥​J⟩∼∑j,j′ΨJ​(j,j′)​(⟨j⁡∥OL∥​j′⟩CLOSE\displaystyle\langle J\lVert\,\sum^{A}_{i=1}O_{L}(i)\,\rVert J\rangle\sim\sum_{j,j^{\prime}}\Psi_{J}(j,j^{\prime})\Bigl(\langle j\lVert O_{L}\rVert j^{\prime}\rangle
OPEN+(−1)j−j′​⟨j′​∥OL∥​j⟩),\displaystyle+(-1)^{j-j^{\prime}}\langle j^{\prime}\lVert O_{L}\rVert j\rangle\Bigr)\,, (25)

where ΨJ​(j,j′)\Psi_{J}(j,j^{\prime}) denotes the one-body density matrix, and the sum is over single-particle total angular momenta j,j′j,j^{\prime} (for simplicity, we have suppressed the sums over radial quantum numbers n,n′n,n^{\prime} and orbital angular momenta l,l′l,l^{\prime}). Therefore, the symmetry properties of the matrix elements under exchange of initial and final states determine the allowed LL contributions to elastic scattering. The relevant operator for SD WIMP-nucleus scattering is ML,L′M_{L,L^{\prime}}, whose matrix elements are given in Appendix C. They transform as

⟨n′​l′​12​j′​∥ML,L​(p​𝐫i)∥​n​l​12​j⟩\displaystyle\langle n^{\prime}l^{\prime}\frac{1}{2}j^{\prime}\lVert M_{L,L}(p{\bf r}_{i})\rVert nl\frac{1}{2}j\rangle
=(−1)j+j′​⟨n​l​12​j​∥ML,L​(p​𝐫i)∥​n′​l′​12​j′⟩,\displaystyle\quad=(-1)^{j+j^{\prime}}\langle nl\frac{1}{2}j\lVert M_{L,L}(p{\bf r}_{i})\rVert n^{\prime}l^{\prime}\frac{1}{2}j^{\prime}\rangle\,, (26)
⟨n′​l′​12​j′​∥ML,L±1​(p​𝐫i)∥​n​l​12​j⟩\displaystyle\langle n^{\prime}l^{\prime}\frac{1}{2}j^{\prime}\lVert M_{L,L\pm 1}(p{\bf r}_{i})\rVert nl\frac{1}{2}j\rangle
=(−1)j−j′​⟨n​l​12​j​∥ML,L±1​(p​𝐫i)∥​n′​l′​12​j′⟩.\displaystyle\quad=(-1)^{j-j^{\prime}}\langle nl\frac{1}{2}j\lVert M_{L,L\pm 1}(p{\bf r}_{i})\rVert n^{\prime}l^{\prime}\frac{1}{2}j^{\prime}\rangle\,. (27)

Therefore, from Eq. (25) it follows that only the multipoles with ML,L±1M_{L,L\pm 1} contribute to elastic scattering. Considering the different multipoles in Eqs. (22)–(24), we thus have

⟨J⁡∥𝒯Lmag5∥​J⟩=0,\langle J\lVert{\mathcal{T}}_{L}^{\mathrm{mag}5}\rVert J\rangle=0\,, (28)

so that the transverse magnetic multipoles do not contribute to elastic scattering.

III.4 Structure factor for elastic SD scattering

As a result, the structure factor for elastic SD WIMP scattering off nuclei is given by [5]

SA​(p)=∑L​ odd(|⟨J⁡∥ℒL5​(p)∥​J⟩|2+|⟨J⁡∥𝒯Lel5​(p)∥​J⟩|2),S_{A}(p)=\sum_{L\text{ odd}}\Bigl(\bigl|\langle J\lVert{\mathcal{L}}_{L}^{5}(p)\rVert J\rangle\bigr|^{2}+\bigl|\langle J\lVert{\mathcal{T}}_{L}^{\mathrm{el}5}(p)\rVert J\rangle\bigr|^{2}\Bigr)\,, (29)

and only odd-LL longitudinal and electric transverse multipoles contribute.

IV Results

IV.1 Spectra

The calculation of the structure factors requires a reliable description of the nuclei involved in the scattering process. We perform state-of-the-art large-scale shell-model calculations of the nuclear states using the code ANTOINE [47]. For each nucleus, we solve the many-body problem in an appropriate valence space, which depends on the nuclear mass region. In all calculations, we use nuclear interactions that have been previously employed in nuclear structure and decay studies. To test the quality of the structure calculations, we first compare the theoretical with the experimental spectra for all relevant isotopes.

IV.1.1 129Xe, 131Xe, 127I

For the heaviest nuclei for SD WIMP scattering, 129Xe, 131Xe and 127I, the valence space for both protons and neutrons comprises the 0​g7/20g_{7/2}, 1​d5/21d_{5/2}, 1​d3/21d_{3/2}, 2​s1/22s_{1/2}, and 0​h11/20h_{11/2} orbitals on top of a 100Sn core. For 131Xe we perform an exact diagonalization in this space. However, in order to make the calculations feasible for 129Xe, the number of particle excitations from the lower-lying 0​g7/20g_{7/2}, 1​d5/21d_{5/2} orbitals into the 1​d3/21d_{3/2}, 2​s1/22s_{1/2}, and 0​h11/20h_{11/2} orbitals was limited to three. With these restrictions the matrix dimension for this space is 3.5×1083.5\times 10^{8}. Similarly, for 127I the number of excitations into the the 1​d3/21d_{3/2}, 2​s1/22s_{1/2}, and 0​h11/20h_{11/2} orbitals was limited to four, leading to a matrix dimension of 4.3×1084.3\times 10^{8}. For this valence space we have used the so-called GCN5082 interaction [48, 49], which is based on a G-matrix with empirical adjustments, mainly in the monopole part, to describe nuclei within this region. The same interaction and valence space have been used to study nuclear structure and double-beta decays in Refs. [48, 49, 50, 51].

Figure 1 shows the excitation energies of the lowest-lying states of 129Xe and 131Xe in comparison with experiment (all energies are measured from the ground state). These spectra have been previously presented in Ref. [15]. In Fig. 2, we show the spectrum of 127I. For all three cases, the experimental ground state and the overall ordering of the excited states are very well described. This represents a clear improvement with respect to previous work [23], and validates the interaction and valence space used. Note that for 127I the spin and parity assignment for some experimental states are not known. These states are absent in our calculated spectra, which suggests that they have significant contributions from orbitals lying outside the valence space considered in the present calculations.

IV.1.2 73Ge

For 73Ge, the valence space for both protons and neutrons comprises the 1​p3/21p_{3/2}, 0​f5/20f_{5/2}, 1​p1/21p_{1/2}, and 0​g9/20g_{9/2} orbitals on top of a 56Ni core. The calculations are performed in the complete space. We compare results for two different interactions, the so-called GCN2850 interaction [48, 49] (Int. 1 in the following) and the RG interaction [52] (Int. 2). Both are also based on a G-matrix, with mainly monopole empirical adjustments for this region. They have been employed in beta and double-beta decay studies, Refs. [48, 49] for Int. 1 and Refs. [52, 53] for Int. 2. The former was also used in a smaller valence space for the description of 73Ge in Ref. [13].

In Fig. 3 we compare the resulting spectra with experiment. We find that the ground state and the overall ordering of states is much better reproduced by the Int. 2 interaction. In particular, the structure of three of the lowest-lying states and the gap between them and the higher-lying states are well described. In contrast, the Int. 1 interaction predicts a 1/2−1/2^{-} ground state, in disagreement with experiment, and the general spacing of the spectrum is not well described. Consequently, the Int. 2 interaction will be the preferred one in this work. Nevertheless, we will also keep the Int. 1 case, in order to study the sensitivity of the structure factor to the different nuclear interactions. It is important to note that the first excited state, which is a 5/2+5/2^{+} state, is at too high excitation energy in both calculations. This suggests that an extended valence space, probably including the higher-lying 1​d5/21d_{5/2} orbital, is needed to account for this state. This was also observed in Ref. [17]. A reliable description of the 5/2+5/2^{+} state will be crucial for the study of inelastic scattering off 73Ge.

IV.1.3 19F, 23Na ,27Al, 29Si

The valence space of the four lighter nuclei 19F, 23Na, 27Al, and 29Si is the s​dsd shell, which comprises the 0​d5/20d_{5/2}, 1​s1/21s_{1/2}, and 0​d3/20d_{3/2} orbitals, with a 16O core. Full calculations in this valence space are easily performed. In previous works [18, 17, 20, 21, 13], the USD interaction [54] was employed. This interaction consists of a best fit to selected nuclei in this mass region. Here, we use the more recent USDB interaction [55], which is an improved version of USD. The difference between the two interactions is small, see Sec. IV.2. In Figs. 4 and 5 the positive-parity excited states of all four nuclei are shown compared to experiment (in the s​dsd shell only positive-parity states can be obtained). The agreement with experiment is very good in all cases, both for the ordering and the quantitative reproduction of the excitation energies.

IV.2 Spin expectation values

In the limit of low momentum transfer, p=0p=0, the structure factor for elastic SD WIMP scattering is given by the proton and neutron spins 𝐒p=∑i=1Z𝝈i/2{\bf S}_{p}=\sum^{Z}_{i=1}{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}/2 and 𝐒n=∑i=1N𝝈i/2{\bf S}_{n}=\sum^{N}_{i=1}{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}/2 in the nucleus [5]:

SA​(0)=14​π​|(a0+a1′)​⟨J⁡∥𝐒p∥​J⟩+(a0−a1′)​⟨J⁡∥𝐒n∥​J⟩|2\displaystyle S_{A}(0)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\bigl|(a_{0}+a_{1}^{\prime})\langle J\lVert{\bf S}_{p}\rVert J\rangle+(a_{0}-a_{1}^{\prime})\langle J\lVert{\bf S}_{n}\rVert J\rangle\bigl|^{2} (30)
=(2​J+1)​(J+1)4​π​J​|(a0+a1′)​⟨𝐒p⟩+(a0−a1′)​⟨𝐒n⟩|2,\displaystyle=\frac{(2J+1)(J+1)}{4\pi J}\bigl|(a_{0}+a_{1}^{\prime})\langle{\bf S}_{p}\rangle+(a_{0}-a_{1}^{\prime})\langle{\bf S}_{n}\rangle\bigl|^{2}\,, (31)

where a1′=a1​(1+δ​a1​(0))a_{1}^{\prime}=a_{1}(1+\delta a_{1}(0)) includes the effects from chiral 2b currents. The spin expectation values are defined as ⟨𝐒n,p⟩=⟨J​M=J​|𝐒n,p3|​J​M=J⟩\langle{\bf S}_{n,p}\rangle=\langle JM=J|{\bf S}^{3}_{n,p}|JM=J\rangle.

We list our calculated spin expectation values ⟨𝐒n,p⟩\langle{\bf S}_{n,p}\rangle in Table 3 in comparison to previous calculations. As expected for odd-mass nuclei with even number of protons (129,131Xe, 73Ge, and 29Si) |⟨𝐒n⟩|≫|⟨𝐒p⟩||\langle{\bf S}_{n}\rangle|\gg|\langle{\bf S}_{p}\rangle|, while for odd-mass nuclei with an even number of neutrons (19F, 23Na ,27Al, and 127I) |⟨𝐒n⟩|≪|⟨𝐒p⟩||\langle{\bf S}_{n}\rangle|\ll|\langle{\bf S}_{p}\rangle|. As a result, the WIMP coupling to the even species will be suppressed. Moreover, the sensitivity to the precise value of the even species spin is very weak when chiral 2b currents are included. This is shown in Sec. IV.3. Chiral 2b currents lead to an interaction of neutrons and protons that overwhelms the direct WIMP coupling to the suppressed spin expectation value, so that the structure factors are almost entirely determined by the dominant ⟨𝐒n/p⟩\langle{\bf S}_{n/p}\rangle (for odd neutron/proton isotopes).

The spin expectation values of the lighter nuclei, 19F, 23Na, 27Al, and 29Si in Table 3 are very close to those of Refs. [18, 17, 20, 21, 13] due to the similarity of the USD and USDB interactions. This indicates that the structure for these nuclei is under good control. For 73Ge we find a weak sensitivity of the dominant ⟨𝐒n⟩\langle{\bf S}_{n}\rangle value comparing the preferred Int. 2 interaction (“This work”) to the Int. 1 interaction. This range is smaller than the one in previous calculations of Refs. [17, 19, 22, 13], suggesting that the latter may have an even larger variation in the spectra due to truncations or deficiencies in the interactions used. Also for the heavier nuclei, 129,131Xe, and 127I, we have performed calculations in the largest spaces to date and with tested interactions. For 129,131Xe, the comparison to previous results is discussed in detail in Ref. [15]. For the dominant ⟨𝐒n⟩\langle{\bf S}_{n}\rangle values for 129,131Xe, and the dominant ⟨𝐒p⟩\langle{\bf S}_{p}\rangle value for 127I, the difference to previous calculations of Refs. [13, 20, 22, 23] is about 25%25\% (and 55%55\% for 131Xe). We attribute these differences to the sizable truncations of the valence spaces in those calculations and because the interactions used have not been as well tested.

IV.3 Structure factors

IV.3.1 Isoscalar/isovector versus proton/neutron

The structure factor SA​(p)S_{A}(p) can be decomposed in terms of its isoscalar and isovector parts Si​j​(p)S_{ij}(p), characterized by the isoscalar and isovector couplings a0a_{0} and a1a_{1}:

SA​(p)=a02​S00​(p)+a0​a1​S01​(p)+a12​S11​(p).S_{A}(p)=a_{0}^{2}\,S_{00}(p)+a_{0}a_{1}S_{01}(p)+a_{1}^{2}\,S_{11}(p)\,. (32)

However, it is common in the literature to use the structure factors Sp​(p)S_{p}(p) and Sn​(p)S_{n}(p), which are referred to as “proton-only” and “neutron-only”, respectively. They are defined by the couplings a0=a1=1a_{0}=a_{1}=1 (“proton-only”) and a0=−a1=1a_{0}=-a_{1}=1 (“neutron-only”) and are thus related to the isoscalar and isovector structure factors by

Sp​(p)\displaystyle S_{p}(p) =S00​(p)+S01​(p)+S11​(p),\displaystyle=S_{00}(p)+S_{01}(p)+S_{11}(p)\,, (33)
Sn​(p)\displaystyle S_{n}(p) =S00​(p)−S01​(p)+S11​(p).\displaystyle=S_{00}(p)-S_{01}(p)+S_{11}(p)\,. (34)

The origin of the “proton/neutron-only” structure factors can be understood from Eq. (31). When 2b currents are neglected, at p=0p=0 the “proton/neutron-only” structure factors are determined entirely by the proton/neutron spin expectation values. Moreover, when the higher-order isovector parts in 1b currents are neglected, this separation also holds for p>0p>0. Because for odd-mass nuclei there is a clear hierarchy of the spin expectation values (with either |⟨𝐒n⟩|≫|⟨𝐒p⟩||\langle{\bf S}_{n}\rangle|\gg|\langle{\bf S}_{p}\rangle| or |⟨𝐒p⟩|≫|⟨𝐒n⟩||\langle{\bf S}_{p}\rangle|\gg|\langle{\bf S}_{n}\rangle|), the proton/neutron decomposition is useful to capture the dominant parts of SA​(p)S_{A}(p). For this reason, and because it is common experimentally, we will also largely consider the proton/neutron decomposition here. This is merely a convenient choice of a0,a1a_{0},a_{1} couplings, but the notation “proton/neutron-only” is misleading, because it does not imply that the coupling is to protons/neutrons only. Strong interactions between nucleons in 2b currents, as well as the isovector nature of pseudo-scalar and other Q2Q^{2} 1b currents, mean that WIMPs effectively couple to protons and neutrons in nuclei. In fact, with 2b currents, both Sp​(p)S_{p}(p) and Sn​(p)S_{n}(p) are determined by the spin distribution of the odd species.

In the following, we present structure factors as a function of u=p2​b2/2u=p^{2}b^{2}/2 with harmonic-oscillator length b=(ℏ/m​ω)1/2b=(\hbar/m\omega)^{1/2} and ℏω=(45A−1/3−25A−2/3)MeV\hbar\omega=(45A^{-1/3}-25A^{-2/3})\,{\rm MeV}. When 2b currents are included, we provide theoretical error bands due to the uncertainties in WIMP currents in nuclei, see Table 2. This takes into account the uncertainties in the low-energy couplings c3,c4c_{3},c_{4} and in the density range ρ=0.10​…​0.12​fm−3\rho=0.10...0.12\,\text{fm}^{-3}.

For 129Xe and 131Xe the predicted isoscalar/isovector structure factors S00​(u),S01​(u)S_{00}(u),S_{01}(u), and S11​(u)S_{11}(u) were discussed in detail in Ref. [15], and they were compared to the previous calculations of Refs. [20, 23] (see also Sec. IV.2). Here, we present in Fig. 6 the proton/neutron structure factors Sp​(u)S_{p}(u). At the 1b current level, the results at p=0p=0 are determined by the spin expectation values. Chiral 2b currents provide important contributions to the structure factors, especially for p≲100​MeVp\lesssim 100\,\text{MeV}, where we find in Fig. 6 a significant increase of Sp​(u)S_{p}(u). This is because with 2b currents, neutrons can contribute to the “proton-only” (a0=a1=1a_{0}=a_{1}=1) coupling due to the axial δ​a1​(p)\delta a_{1}(p) contribution in Eq. (31). For Sn​(u)S_{n}(u), 2b currents lead to a small reduction in the structure factor, depending on the momentum transfer. This is caused by the combined effect of the axial δ​a1​(p)\delta a_{1}(p) and the pseudo-scalar δ​a1P​(p)\delta a_{1}^{P}(p) contributions. To better understand how these different contributions enter, we study a multipole decomposition of the structure factors.

IV.3.2 Multipole decomposition

In Fig. 7 we show the transverse/longitudinal decomposition of the results with 1b as well as 1b plus 2b currents for the isovector structure factor S11​(u)S_{11}(u) of 131Xe (the long-range 2b currents are isovector). The different 2b current contributions can be clearly seen in Fig. 7. In the middle panel, where only the transverse electric multipoles are taken into account, 2b currents reduce the 1b result due to the negative axial δ​a1​(p)\delta a_{1}(p) values in Table 2. We observe that the relative reduction depends on uu and becomes more important at higher momentum transfer. The bottom panel shows the longitudinal multipoles, where both axial δ​a1​(p)\delta a_{1}(p) and pseudo-scalar δ​a1P​(p)\delta a_{1}^{P}(p) 2b current contributions enter. At zero momentum transfer we find a reduction of the structure factor, driven by δ​a1​(p)\delta a_{1}(p), but at u∼0.7u\sim 0.7, p∼100​MeVp\sim 100\,\text{MeV}, this turns into an enhancement due to δ​a1P​(p)\delta a_{1}^{P}(p). In the upper panel, the full 1b plus 2b band is given, where the final reduction or enhancement over the 1b result, for a given uu value, depends on the relative impact of the transverse electric and longitudinal multipoles.

It is interesting to study the transverse/longitudinal decomposition at the 1b level, as shown in Fig. 8 for Sn​(u)S_{n}(u) and Sp​(u)S_{p}(u) of 131Xe. While both multipoles contribute to Sn​(u)S_{n}(u) (their relative importance depends on uu), Sp​(u)S_{p}(u) is completely dominated by the longitudinal multipoles except at p=0p=0. In 131Xe almost all of the spin is carried by neutrons, so Sp​(0)S_{p}(0) is very small at the 1b level. However, for p>0p>0 the (isovector) pseudo-scalar currents allow neutrons to contribute to Sp​(u)S_{p}(u), leading to a steep increase in the longitudinal contribution to Sp​(u)S_{p}(u). Because pseudo-scalar currents only contribute to the longitudinal multipoles, the transverse part from the protons also remains very small for p>0p>0.

Another way to decompose the structure factors is in terms of the different LL values of the multipoles. Because the ground state of 129Xe is 1/2+1/2^{+}, only L=1L=1 contributes. For 131Xe, with a 3/2+3/2^{+} ground state, L=1L=1 and L=3L=3 multipoles enter (even-LL multipoles are forbidden due to parity, see Sec. III.2). The LL decomposition of the 131Xe structure factor Sn​(u)S_{n}(u) is shown in Fig. 9, for simplicity at the 1b current level. We observe that the L=3L=3 multipoles dominate for 1.5≲u≲51.5\lesssim u\lesssim 5. As a result, the structure factors fall off considerably more slowly for 131Xe compared to 129Xe, where only L=1L=1 contributes.

IV.3.3 73Ge

Figure 10 shows the structure factors for 73Ge for the different Int. 1 and Int. 2 interactions (the latter is preferred based on the spectra, see Fig. 3). The structure factor Sn​(u)S_{n}(u) differs by less than 10%10\% between the two interactions. At the 1b current level, Sp​(u)S_{p}(u) for low momentum transfers is substantially smaller for Int. 1, due to the very small ⟨𝐒p⟩\langle{\bf S}_{p}\rangle value. However, when 2b currents are included, also for Sp​(u)S_{p}(u) the contributions from neutrons are dominant, which translates to similar structure factors for the two interactions. This is because of the similar ⟨𝐒n⟩\langle{\bf S}_{n}\rangle values (see Table 3) combined with the neutron-proton coupling through 2b currents.

IV.3.4 127I, 19F, 23Na, 27Al, 29Si

In Figs. 11, 12, and 13, we show the structure factors Sn​(u)S_{n}(u) and Sp​(u)S_{p}(u) for 127I, 19F, 23Na, 27Al, and 29Si at the 1b current level and including 2b currents. The dominant structure factor is the one for the odd species. Therefore, for 29Si Sn​(u)S_{n}(u) dominates, while for the other isotopes Sp​(u)S_{p}(u) is the main component. All the features discussed for 131Xe in Sec. IV.3.2 translate to these isotopes as well: The structure factors for the nondominant “proton/neutron-only” couplings are strongly increased when 2b currents are included. For the dominant structure factor, 2b currents produce a reduction, by about 10%−30%10\%-30\% at low momentum transfers, which at large uu can turn into a weak enhancement due to the 2b current contribution to the pseudo-scalar currents. This is most clearly seen for 19F in the top panel of Fig. 12, where we also show the isoscalar/isovector structure factors S00​(u)S_{00}(u), S01​(u)S_{01}(u), and S11​(u)S_{11}(u). Note that the structure factor S01​(u)S_{01}(u) vanishes at the point where Sp​(u)S_{p}(u) and Sn​(u)S_{n}(u) cross.

V Conclusions and outlook

This work presents a comprehensive derivation of SD WIMP scattering off nuclei based on chiral EFT, including one-body currents to order Q2Q^{2} and the long-range Q3Q^{3} two-body currents due to pion exchange, which are predicted in chiral EFT. Two-body currents are the leading corrections to the couplings of WIMPs to single nucleons, assumed in all previous studies. Combined with detailed Appendixes, we have presented the general formalism necessary to describe both elastic and inelastic WIMP-nucleus scattering.

We have performed state-of-the-art large-scale shell-model calculations for all nonzero-spin nuclei relevant to direct dark matter detection, using the largest valence spaces accessible with nuclear interactions that have been tested in nuclear structure and decay studies. The comparison of theoretical and experimental spectra demonstrate a good description of these isotopes. We have calculated the structure factors for elastic SD WIMP scattering for all cases using chiral EFT currents, including theoretical error bands due to the nuclear uncertainties of WIMP currents in nuclei. Fits for the structure factors are given in Appendix D.

We have studied in detail the role of two-body currents, the contributions of different multipole operators, and the issue of proton/neutron versus isoscalar/isovector decompositions of the structure factors. The long-range two-body currents reduce the isovector parts of the structure factor at low momentum transfer, while they can lead to a weak enhancement at higher momentum transfers. Moreover, we have shown that for odd-neutron (odd-proton) nuclei, two-body currents lead to a significant increase of the “proton-only” (“neutron-only”) structure factors, because of strong interactions between nucleons through two-body currents that allow the odd species carrying most of the spin to contribute. This implies that WIMPs effectively couple to protons and neutrons in nuclei, so that the notation “proton/neutron-only” is misleading. In fact, with 2b currents, both “proton/neutron-only” structure factors are determined by the spin distribution of the odd species.

Future improvements of the nuclear physics of dark matter detection includes developing shell-model interactions based on chiral EFT, where the present frontier are semi-magic nuclei up to the calcium region [56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61], ab-initio benchmarks for the lightest isotope 19F, and expanding the valences spaces (especially for germanium). In addition, a full treatment of the one- and two-body currents would require to renormalize them to the valence space of the many-body calculation, which can lead to additional contributions to the currents. This and going beyond the normal-ordering approximation will be pursued in future work. Moreover, we plan to investigate other responses [13] based on the same large-scale nuclear-structure calculations presented here.

We start from the Lagrangian density for spin-dependent WIMP-nucleus scattering Eq. (1). WIMPs are expected to be nonrelativistic with velocities of the order v/c∼10−3v/c\sim 10^{-3}, so the time components of the currents can be neglected. The specific form of the multipoles depends on the form of the WIMP currents 𝐉iA​(𝐫){\bf J}^{A}_{i}({\bf r}). They contain either axial-vector terms [𝝈i{\bm{\sigma}_{i}}] or pseudo-scalar ones [(𝐩⋅𝝈i)​𝐩({\bf p}\cdot{\bm{\sigma}_{i}}){\bf p}]. For axial-vector currents, the response will be proportional to the following operator

ML,L′M​(p​𝐫i)\displaystyle M^{M}_{L,L^{\prime}}(p{\bf r}_{i}) =jL′​(p​ri)​𝐘L​L​1M​(𝐫i)⋅𝝈i,\displaystyle=j_{L^{\prime}}(pr_{i}){\bf Y}^{M}_{LL1}({\bf r}_{i})\cdot{\bm{\sigma}_{i}}\,,
=jL′​(p​ri)​∑m​λ⟨L′​m​1​λ|L′​1​L​M⟩​YL′​m​(𝐫i)​σi1​λ=jL′​(p​ri)​[YL′​(𝐫i)​𝝈i]L.\displaystyle=j_{L^{\prime}}(pr_{i})\sum_{m\lambda}\braket{L^{\prime}m1\lambda|L^{\prime}1LM}Y_{L^{\prime}m}({\bf r}_{i})\,\sigma_{i}^{1\lambda}=j_{L^{\prime}}(pr_{i})\bigl[Y_{L^{\prime}}({\bf r}_{i}){\bm{\sigma}}_{i}\bigr]^{L}\,. (68)

Pseudo-Scalar currents, which are proportional to the momentum transfer 𝐩{\bf p}, only contribute to the longitudinal multipoles (see Eq. (54)). Moreover, in these we can replace (𝐩⋅𝝈i)​𝐩({\bf p}\cdot{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}){\bf p} by p2​𝝈ip^{2}{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}, because of

(𝐩⋅𝝈i)​𝐩=p2​𝝈i+𝐩×(𝐩×𝝈i),({\bf p}\cdot{\bm{\sigma}_{i}}){\bf p}=p^{2}{\bm{\sigma}_{i}}+{\bf p}\times({\bf p}\times{\bm{\sigma}_{i}})\,, (69)

and the second term is perpendicular to 𝐩{\bf p}, so it vanishes for the longitudinal multipoles. As a result, pseudo-scalar currents can also be expressed in terms of ML,L′M​(p​𝐫i)M^{M}_{L,L^{\prime}}(p{\bf r}_{i}).

In summary, including chiral 2b currents at the normal-ordered one-body level in Eq. (19), we have for the multipoles

ℒL5​(p)=\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{L}^{5}(p)= i2​L+1​∑i=1A12​[a0+a1​τi3​(1+δ​a1​(p)−2​gπ​p​n​Fπ​p22​m​gA​(p2+mπ2)+δ​a1P​(p))]\displaystyle\frac{i}{\sqrt{2L+1}}\sum^{A}_{i=1}\frac{1}{2}\biggl[a_{0}+a_{1}\tau^{3}_{i}\Bigl(1+\delta a_{1}(p)-\frac{2g_{\pi pn}F_{\pi}p^{2}}{2mg_{A}(p^{2}+m^{2}_{\pi})}+\delta a_{1}^{P}(p)\Bigr)\biggr]
×[L+1​ML,L+1​(p​𝐫i)+L​ML,L−1​(p​𝐫i)],\displaystyle\times\Bigl[\sqrt{L+1}M_{L,L+1}(p{\bf r}_{i})+\sqrt{L}M_{L,L-1}(p{\bf r}_{i})\Bigr]\,, (70)
𝒯Lel5​(p)=\displaystyle{\mathcal{T}}_{L}^{\mathrm{el}5}(p)= i2​L+1​∑i=1A12​[a0+a1​τi3​(1−2​p2ΛA2+δ​a1​(p))]​[−L​ML,L+1​(p​𝐫i)+L+1​ML,L−1​(p​𝐫i)],\displaystyle\frac{i}{\sqrt{2L+1}}\sum^{A}_{i=1}\frac{1}{2}\biggl[a_{0}+a_{1}\tau^{3}_{i}\Bigl(1-2\frac{p^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}_{A}}+\delta a_{1}(p)\Bigr)\biggr]\Bigl[-\sqrt{L}M_{L,L+1}(p{\bf r}_{i})+\sqrt{L+1}M_{L,L-1}(p{\bf r}_{i})\Bigr], (71)
𝒯Lmag5​(p)=\displaystyle{\mathcal{T}}_{L}^{\mathrm{mag}5}(p)= ∑i=1A12​[a0+a1​τi3​(1−2​p2ΛA2+δ​a1​(p))]​ML,L​(p​𝐫i).\displaystyle\sum^{A}_{i=1}\frac{1}{2}\biggl[a_{0}+a_{1}\tau^{3}_{i}\Bigl(1-2\frac{p^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}_{A}}+\delta a_{1}(p)\Bigr)\biggr]M_{L,L}(p{\bf r}_{i})\,. (72)

Note that the p2/ΛA2p^{2}/\Lambda_{A}^{2} terms cancel in the longitudinal response and only contribute to the transverse multipoles.

Appendix C Reduced matrix elements of ML,L′​(p​𝐫i)M_{L,L^{\prime}}(p{\bf r}_{i})

=⟨n′​l′|​jL′​|n​l⟩​⟨n′​l′|​|YL′|​|n​l⟩​⟨12|​|𝝈i|​|12⟩​[(2​j+1)​(2​j′+1)​(2​L+1)]12​{l′lL′12121j′jL}\displaystyle=\bra{n^{\prime}l^{\prime}}j_{L^{\prime}}\ket{nl}\bra{n^{\prime}l^{\prime}}\!|Y_{L^{\prime}}|\!\ket{nl}\bra{\frac{1}{2}}\!|{\bm{\sigma}}_{i}|\!\ket{\frac{1}{2}}\bigl[(2j+1)(2j^{\prime}+1)(2L+1)\bigr]^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}l^{\prime}&l&L^{\prime}\\ \frac{1}{2}&\frac{1}{2}&1\\ j^{\prime}&j&L\end{array}\right\}

×(l′L′l000)​{l′lL′12121j′jL}.\displaystyle\quad\times\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}l^{\prime}&L^{\prime}&l\\ 0&0&0\end{array}\right)\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}l^{\prime}&l&L^{\prime}\\ \frac{1}{2}&\frac{1}{2}&1\\ j^{\prime}&j&L\end{array}\right\}\,.

Appendix D Fits of the structure factors

In Tables 4-8 we give fits for the isoscalar/isovector and “neutron-only”/“proton-only” decompositions of the structure factors of all isotopes studied in this work. Results are given including 1b+2b currents.
